topics.h: Why does a rainbow appear after rain? Why does a ball always come back down? Asking 'why?' is where science begins!
p: Science is a way of finding out how the world around us works.
It begins with curiosity: noticing things and wondering about them.
Science is not just a school subject or a list of facts; it is a way of thinking and checking ideas.
Scientists test their ideas and change them when new evidence shows they were wrong.
Anyone can think like a scientist: a farmer, a cook, a doctor or you!

ex.q: Meera says, 'Science is only about lab coats and test tubes.' Is she right?
st: Think of where people use scientific thinking: farmers checking soil, cooks testing recipes, doctors finding the cause of an illness.
Science is a way of observing, asking questions and testing ideas.
This can happen in a kitchen, a garden or a playground, not only in a lab.
ex.a: No. Science is a way of thinking and finding out that we can use anywhere.

topics.rl: When you wonder why milk boils over, why curd sets faster in summer, or why your shadow is long in the evening, you are thinking like a scientist.

rv.summary: Science is a way of finding out how the world works. It starts with curiosity, and scientists test their ideas and change them when evidence shows they were wrong.

topics.h: A good scientist is like a detective: they notice tiny clues that others miss!
p: Observing means using our senses (seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, tasting) carefully to notice things.
Never taste or smell unknown things to observe them; safety comes first.
Instruments like a magnifying glass, a ruler or a thermometer help us observe more exactly.
Good observations are recorded in a notebook with dates, drawings and numbers.
Good questions come from observations, for example: 'Why are the leaves of this plant drooping?'

ex.q: Riya sees that the curd at her nani's house in Jaipur sets faster in May than in January. What question could she ask?
st: Write down the observation: curd sets faster in May.
Think about what is different in May: it is much warmer.
Turn it into a question that can be tested.
ex.a: Does warmth make curd set faster?

topics.rl: Birdwatchers in India note the birds they see, like the kingfisher or the peacock, with the date and place. Their careful records help scientists know where birds live and travel.

topics.h: Is your guess right or wrong? There is only one way to find out: test it!
p: The scientific method is a step-by-step way of finding answers.
Steps: observe → ask a question → make a guess (hypothesis) → test it with an experiment → look at the results → draw a conclusion.
A hypothesis is a smart guess that can be tested.
In a fair test, we change only one thing and keep everything else the same.
If the results do not support the guess, we make a new guess and test again. That is not failure; it is learning!

ex.q: Dev thinks sugar dissolves faster in warm water than in cold water. How can he test it fairly? (Use warm tap water only, with an adult nearby.)
st: Take two same-sized glasses with the same amount of water: one warm, one cold.
Add one spoon of sugar to each at the same time and stir both the same way.
Change only the temperature of the water; keep everything else the same.
Observe which glass becomes clear first and write down the result.
ex.a: If the sugar disappears first in the warm water, his guess is supported: warm water dissolves sugar faster.

topics.rl: Doctors testing a new medicine, and farmers trying a new way of watering, use these same steps: guess, test fairly, and check the results.

topics.h: From tiny ants to huge elephants, from soft grass to giant banyan trees: India is bursting with living things!
p: Biodiversity means the huge variety of living things in a place.
India is one of the world's richest countries in plant and animal variety; the Western Ghats and the Himalayas are full of life.

Plants can be grouped by height and stem: herbs (short, soft green stem, like wheat and mint), shrubs (woody stem with branches near the ground, like rose and hibiscus) and trees (tall, with a thick woody trunk, like neem and mango).
Climbers (like money plant and grapevine) climb up with support; creepers (like watermelon and pumpkin) spread along the ground.
Animals also vary: they live in different places, move in different ways and eat different foods.

ex.q: A plant in Meena's garden is about her height. It has a hard, woody stem and many branches starting just above the soil. What kind of plant is it?
st: Herbs are short with soft, green stems; this stem is woody, so it is not a herb.
Trees have one thick trunk with branches high above the ground; this plant branches near the soil.
Medium height, woody stem, branches near the base: that matches a shrub.
ex.a: It is a shrub, like a rose or hibiscus bush.

topics.rl: On a walk in a park you may spot a peepal tree, a hibiscus shrub, grass, a money plant climbing a wall, squirrels, mynas and butterflies, all in one place. That is biodiversity!

rv.summary: Biodiversity is the huge variety of living things in a place. Plants are grouped as herbs, shrubs and trees by height and stem, and as climbers or creepers by how they grow.

traps: Don't call a money plant a creeper; it climbs with support, so it is a climber.
A shrub's stem is woody, not soft like a herb's.

topics.h: Imagine a library with all books thrown in one heap. Grouping living things is like arranging that library!
p: We group living things by features they share, which makes them easier to study.
Leaves can have net-like veins (reticulate venation, like mango and hibiscus) or parallel veins (parallel venation, like grass, banana and wheat).
Roots can be a taproot (one main root with side roots, like mustard and mango) or fibrous roots (many thin roots of similar size, like wheat, maize and grass).
Plants with parallel venation usually have fibrous roots; plants with net-like venation usually have a taproot.
Seeds of gram and rajma split into two parts (dicots); seeds of maize and wheat have one part (monocots). Animals can be grouped by where they live, how they move or whether they have a backbone.

ex.q: Neha finds a plant whose leaves have parallel veins. What kind of roots does it most likely have?
st: Parallel venation is found in plants like grass, wheat and maize.
These plants have many thin roots coming out from the base of the stem.
So parallel venation usually goes with fibrous roots.
ex.a: Fibrous roots

topics.rl: Gardeners and farmers group plants to decide how to grow them. Doctors and zoo keepers group animals to understand how to care for them.

rv.summary: We group living things by shared features. Leaves have net-like or parallel veins, roots are taproots or fibrous, and seeds may split into two parts (dicots) or not (monocots).

traps: Don't mix up the pairs: parallel venation goes with fibrous roots, not taproots.
A taproot has one main root, not many roots of the same size.

topics.h: Why does a camel not mind the hot sand, and a fish not drown in water? Nature has given each one special tools!
p: An adaptation is a special feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat (home).
Camel (Thar desert): long legs keep its body away from hot sand, wide padded feet do not sink in sand, and its hump stores fat. It can go many days without drinking water.
Cactus: leaves are turned into spines that reduce water loss; the thick green stem stores water and makes food.
Fish: a streamlined body and fins for swimming, and gills to take in oxygen dissolved in water.
Mountains: deodar and pine trees are cone-shaped with sloping branches so snow slides off; yaks and snow leopards have thick fur to keep warm. Lotus leaves float on water.

ex.q: A camel's hump is often said to be a water tank. Is that correct?
st: Think about what a hump is made of: it is a store of fat.
When food is scarce, the camel's body uses this fat for energy.
Camels can go many days without water for other reasons, such as losing very little water from their bodies.
ex.a: No. The hump stores fat, not water.

topics.rl: When you visit Ladakh you may see yaks with shaggy coats, and in Rajasthan, camels carrying people across sand dunes. Each animal is built for its home.

rv.summary: An adaptation is a special feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat, like a camel's long legs, a cactus's spines, a fish's gills or a pine tree's sloping branches.

topics.ch: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
topics.h: Your plate of dal, rice and sabzi is actually a team of tiny helpers. Each one has a job to do in your body!
p: Nutrients are the parts of food our body needs to stay healthy.
Carbohydrates (rice, wheat roti, potato, millets like ragi and bajra) give us energy. Fats (ghee, butter, oil, nuts) give even more energy.
Proteins (dal, rajma, milk, paneer, eggs, fish, soybean) are body-building foods: they help us grow and repair the body.
Vitamins and minerals (fruits, vegetables, milk) protect us from diseases and keep the body working well.
Dietary fibre (roughage) in whole grains, fruits and vegetables helps the body get rid of undigested food. Water helps carry nutrients and remove wastes as sweat and urine.

ex.q: Aman plays football for two hours every evening. Which nutrient does he mainly need for energy, and from which food?
st: Running and kicking use a lot of energy.
Carbohydrates and fats are energy-giving nutrients.
Foods like rice, roti, potato and millets are rich in carbohydrates.
ex.a: Carbohydrates, from foods like rice, roti and millets (fats also give energy).

topics.rl: In school, with a teacher, a drop of dilute iodine solution on a potato slice turns it blue-black, showing starch (a carbohydrate). Rubbing a groundnut on paper leaves an oily patch that light shines through, showing fat. Never taste or play with lab chemicals.

rv.summary: Nutrients are the parts of food our body needs: carbohydrates and fats give energy, proteins build and repair the body, vitamins and minerals protect us, and fibre and water keep the body working well.

topics.ch: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
topics.h: A cricket team needs batters, bowlers and a keeper. Your meal also needs a full team of nutrients!
p: A balanced diet has all the nutrients in the right amounts, along with fibre and water.
How much food we need depends on our age, how active we are and our health. A growing child and a farmer need plenty of energy.
Indian meals like dal-chawal with sabzi and curd, or roti with dal and salad, can be nicely balanced.
Millets like ragi, jowar and bajra are nutritious grains. The United Nations named 2023 the International Year of Millets.
Mindful eating means eating slowly, chewing well, stopping when full, eating fresh home-cooked food, eating less junk food and not wasting food.

ex.q: Priya's lunch is only puri and aloo sabzi, with a glass of cola. How can she make it balanced?
st: Puri (fried) and potato give carbohydrates and fat, which are energy.
Missing: protein, enough vitamins and minerals, and fibre. Cola adds lots of sugar.
Add dal or curd for protein, a salad or green vegetable for vitamins and fibre, and drink water instead of cola.
ex.a: Add dal or curd, a green vegetable or salad, and choose water instead of cola.

topics.rl: Each region of India has its own balanced meals: idli-sambar in the south, dal-baati in Rajasthan, fish-rice in Bengal and makki roti with sarson saag in Punjab.

rv.summary: A balanced diet has all the nutrients in the right amounts, with fibre and water. Mindful eating means eating slowly, stopping when full, eating fresh food, less junk food and not wasting food.

topics.ch: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
topics.h: If your body misses one tiny vitamin for a long time, it can show signs like weak bones or bleeding gums. Good food fixes it!
p: A deficiency disease happens when the body does not get enough of a nutrient for a long time.
Vitamin A: poor eyesight, especially night blindness (eat carrots, papaya, mango, milk). Vitamin B1: beriberi, weak muscles (eat whole grains, pulses).
Vitamin C: scurvy, bleeding gums (eat amla, guava, oranges, lemons). Vitamin D: rickets, soft and bent bones (sunlight, milk, eggs, fish).
Calcium: weak bones and teeth (milk, curd, ragi). Iodine: goitre, a swelling in the neck (iodised salt). Iron: anaemia, feeling tired and weak (green leafy vegetables, pulses).
Deficiency diseases can be prevented by eating a balanced diet.

ex.q: Raju's gums bleed often. His doctor says he needs more of a certain vitamin. Which vitamin, and what should he eat?
st: Bleeding gums are a sign of scurvy.
Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C.
Vitamin C is found in citrus fruits, amla and guava.
ex.a: Vitamin C; he should eat amla, guava, oranges or lemons.

topics.rl: Common table salt in India is often iodised to prevent goitre, and many children get vitamin D by playing in the morning sunshine.

rv.summary: A deficiency disease happens when the body lacks a nutrient for a long time, like scurvy (vitamin C), rickets (vitamin D) or goitre (iodine). A balanced diet prevents them.

topics.h: Why does a fridge magnet stick to the fridge door but not to a wooden table? Let's find out!
p: A magnet attracts (pulls) some materials towards itself.
Materials attracted by a magnet are magnetic materials: iron, nickel and cobalt (and things made mostly of iron).
Materials not attracted by a magnet are non-magnetic: wood, plastic, rubber, glass, paper, cloth, and metals like copper, aluminium, gold and silver.
Not every metal is magnetic! A copper wire or aluminium foil is not pulled by a magnet.
Long ago, people found a natural magnet called magnetite (lodestone), a rock that attracts iron. Today most magnets are made by people, in shapes like bar, U-shaped (horseshoe), ring and disc.

ex.q: Kavya mixes iron pins and plastic beads by mistake. How can she separate them quickly?
st: Iron is a magnetic material; plastic is not.
Move a magnet over the mixture.
The iron pins stick to the magnet and the plastic beads stay behind.
ex.a: Use a magnet to pick up the iron pins.

topics.rl: Scrap dealers (kabadiwalas) and recycling plants use big magnets to separate iron scrap from other waste.

rv.summary: A magnet attracts magnetic materials like iron, nickel and cobalt. Wood, plastic, glass and metals like copper and aluminium are non-magnetic. Magnetite is a natural magnet.

topics.h: Two magnets can hug each other or push each other away. It all depends on which ends meet!
p: Every magnet has two poles: a north pole (N) and a south pole (S).
The attraction of a magnet is strongest near its poles. Iron filings collect most at the ends of a bar magnet.
Like poles repel (N–N or S–S push apart). Unlike poles attract (N–S pull together).
A freely hanging bar magnet always comes to rest pointing in the north–south direction.
If you break a magnet, each piece still has both a north and a south pole. You can never get a magnet with just one pole!

ex.q: Rahul brings the N pole of one bar magnet near the N pole of another. What will he feel? What if he turns one magnet around?
st: N and N are like poles.
Like poles repel, so he will feel the magnets pushing apart.
If he turns one magnet, N faces S. Unlike poles attract, so they pull together.
ex.a: First they repel; after turning one magnet around, they attract.

topics.rl: Magnetic toys and the doors of some cupboards use attraction between unlike poles to snap shut.

topics.t: The compass and caring for magnets
topics.h: Lost in a forest with no phone? A tiny magnetic needle can show you the way!
p: A magnetic compass has a small magnetic needle that can turn freely. It comes to rest pointing north–south.
The north-pointing end of the needle is usually painted or marked so we can read the direction.
Sailors and travellers used compasses to find directions. Sailors and pilots still carry them.
We can make a magnet: stroke an iron nail many times from one end to the other with one pole of a magnet, always in the same direction.
Magnets lose their magnetism if heated, hammered or dropped. Store bar magnets in pairs with unlike poles side by side, with pieces of soft iron (keepers) across the ends.

ex.q: The marked north end of Ishaan's compass needle points towards the big banyan tree near his house. In which direction is the tree from him?
st: A compass needle settles in the north–south direction.
Check the marked (north) end of the needle.
The marked end points to the banyan tree, so the tree lies to the north of him.
ex.a: The tree is to the north of Ishaan.

topics.rl: Ships crossing the Arabian Sea and trekkers in the Himalayas carry compasses, because a compass needs no battery or signal.

topics.h: If you measure a table with your handspan and your little brother measures it with his, you'll get different answers. Who is right?
p: Long ago people measured length with body parts: handspan, cubit (elbow to fingertip), foot, pace (step) and angul (finger width). In ancient India, units like angul and dhanush were used.
Body measures differ from person to person, so the same object gives different results.
So the world agreed on standard units. The SI unit (International System of Units) of length is the metre (m).
1 metre (m) = 100 centimetres (cm); 1 centimetre = 10 millimetres (mm); 1 kilometre (km) = 1000 metres.
We choose the unit to suit the length: mm for a pencil tip, cm for a book, m for a room, km for the distance between cities.

ex.q: Tanvi's ribbon is 2 m 35 cm long. How long is it in centimetres?
st: 1 m = 100 cm, so 2 m = 200 cm.
Add the extra 35 cm: 200 + 35.
ex.a: 235 cm

topics.rl: Shopkeepers measure cloth in metres, road signs show distances in kilometres, and your school ruler shows centimetres and millimetres.

topics.h: A ruler is only as good as the person using it. A tiny slip of the eye can change your answer!
p: Place the scale along the length of the object, touching it.
Start from the zero mark. If the zero mark is broken, start from another full mark (like 1 cm) and subtract it from the final reading.
Keep your eye directly above the point you are reading. Looking from the side gives a wrong reading.
To measure a curved line, lay a thread along it, mark the ends, straighten the thread and measure it with a scale.
Choose the right tool: a ruler for a book, a measuring tape for your waist or a tree trunk, a metre scale for a door.

ex.q: Sameer's ruler has a broken edge, so he places a pencil starting at the 2.0 cm mark. The other end is at 11.5 cm. How long is the pencil?
st: The pencil starts at 2.0 cm, not at 0.
Length = end reading − start reading.
ex.a: 9.5 cm

topics.rl: Tailors use a soft measuring tape around your shoulders and waist, and carpenters use a metal tape to measure wood before cutting.

topics.h: A cricket ball flies, a fan spins, a swing goes back and forth. Everything is moving, but in different ways!
p: An object is in motion if its position changes with time compared to its surroundings; otherwise it is at rest.
Linear motion: moving along a straight line, like a train on a straight track, a falling stone, or a sprinter in a 100 m race.
Circular motion: moving along a circle around a centre, like the tip of a fan blade, a giant wheel at a mela, or a stone tied to a string and whirled.
Periodic motion: a motion that repeats itself after fixed intervals of time, like a swinging pendulum, a jhula going to and fro, or the hands of a clock.
Some motions are of more than one type. A fan blade moves in a circle and repeats again and again, so it is both circular and periodic.

ex.q: What type of motion does a child on a swing (jhula) have?
st: The swing goes forward and comes back to the same point.
It repeats this to-and-fro movement again and again, taking about the same time for each swing.
A motion that repeats after fixed time intervals is periodic.
ex.a: Periodic (to-and-fro, or oscillatory) motion

topics.rl: At a Dussehra or Diwali mela you can spot all three: a toy train on a straight track (linear), a giant wheel (circular) and a pendulum-like boat ride swinging to and fro (periodic).

topics.h: Your tiffin box, your chair and your bangles are all objects. But what are they made of? That's the material!
p: An object is a thing (like a spoon or a chair). A material is what it is made of (like steel, wood, plastic or glass).
One object can be made from different materials: a chair can be wooden, plastic or metal. One material can make many objects: wood makes chairs, doors and pencils.
Appearance: materials that shine, like gold, silver, copper and aluminium foil, are called lustrous. Wood, paper, cloth and chalk are non-lustrous.
Metals can lose their shine in air and moisture; a copper vessel turns dull but shines again after cleaning.
Hardness: hard materials like iron and stone are difficult to scratch or press. Soft materials like cotton and sponge can be pressed easily.

ex.q: Nisha has a piece of cotton and a piece of stone. She tries to press both with her fingers. Which is hard and which is soft?
st: The cotton gets squeezed easily when pressed.
The stone does not change at all when pressed.
A material that is easily pressed or scratched is soft; one that is not is hard.
ex.a: Stone is hard; cotton is soft.

topics.h: Sugar disappears in water, oil floats on top, and you can see through glass but not through a wall. Materials behave differently!
p: Soluble materials dissolve (mix completely) in water, like sugar and salt. Insoluble ones do not, like sand, chalk powder and sawdust.
Some liquids mix with water (lemon juice, vinegar); some do not (oil forms a layer on top).
Some objects float on water (a dry leaf, a piece of wood, a cork); others sink (a stone, an iron nail, a glass marble).
Transparent materials let us see clearly through them (clear glass, clean water, air).
Translucent materials let us see only partly (butter paper, frosted glass, oiled paper). Opaque materials do not let us see through at all (wood, cardboard, a metal sheet).

ex.q: Raj adds a spoon of sand and a spoon of salt to two glasses of water and stirs. What will he see?
st: Salt is soluble in water, so it disappears from view.
Sand is insoluble, so it does not dissolve.
The sand settles at the bottom of the glass.
ex.a: The salt dissolves; the sand settles at the bottom without dissolving.

topics.rl: Windows use transparent glass to let light in, bathroom windows often use translucent frosted glass for privacy, and doors are opaque.

topics.h: If you had to build a kite, would you use paper or iron? Choosing the right material is a superpower!
p: We group materials by their properties: lustrous or dull, hard or soft, soluble or insoluble, floats or sinks, transparent, translucent or opaque.
Grouping helps us study materials and find what we need quickly.
We choose a material for a job based on its properties: glass for windows (transparent), iron for gates (hard and strong), cotton for summer clothes (soft and comfortable).
One material can belong to many groups: glass is transparent, hard and insoluble in water.
Reusing and recycling materials like paper, glass and metal saves resources.

ex.q: Why are cooking pans usually made of metal and their handles of plastic or wood?
st: A pan must get hot quickly and evenly to cook food; metals let heat pass through easily.
The handle must stay cool enough to hold safely.
Plastic and wood do not let heat pass through easily.
ex.a: Metal for the pan to heat the food; plastic or wood for the handle so it stays safe to hold.

topics.rl: Potters choose soft wet clay to shape diyas and matkas, which become hard after baking. Builders choose hard bricks and stone for walls.

topics.h: Can your hands lie to you? Try this and see: the same water can feel warm to one hand and cool to the other!
p: We often say things are hot, warm, cool or cold. Temperature tells us exactly how hot or cold something is.
Our sense of touch is not reliable for judging temperature.

Try this (with an adult): keep one hand in cool tap water and the other in comfortably warm (not hot) water for a minute. Then put both in normal tap water. The 'cool' hand feels it as warm, and the 'warm' hand feels it as cool!
Never test very hot water, a hot iron or a stove with your hand; it can burn you.
To know temperature correctly and safely, we use a thermometer.

ex.q: Two friends dip their hands into the same bucket of water. Simran says 'warm!' and Aditya says 'cool!'. How is this possible?
st: Just before, Simran had her hand in cold water and Aditya had his hand in warm water.
Our skin compares the new water with what it felt just before.
So the same water feels different to each of them.
ex.a: Touch depends on what the hand felt before, so it is not reliable. A thermometer gives the true temperature.

topics.rl: Mothers often check a child's forehead for fever by touch, but a doctor always uses a thermometer to be sure.

topics.h: A thermometer is like a truthful friend: it never says 'it feels warm', it tells you the exact number!
p: A clinical thermometer measures body temperature. Its range is usually 35 °C to 42 °C.
The normal temperature of the human body is about 37 °C. A temperature above this may mean a fever.
A laboratory thermometer measures the temperature of other things like water. Its range is usually −10 °C to 110 °C.
Digital thermometers show the reading as numbers on a screen. Older thermometers had mercury, which is poisonous, so digital ones are now preferred.

Good habits: wash the thermometer before and after use; hold it away from the tip; for a lab thermometer, keep the bulb in the liquid without touching the container and read it while it is still in the liquid.

ex.q: Why should a clinical thermometer NOT be used to measure the temperature of boiling water?
st: A clinical thermometer reads only up to about 42 °C.
Boiling water is at about 100 °C, far above that range.
The thermometer could break, and it cannot show the reading.
ex.a: Its range (35 °C to 42 °C) is too small. Use a laboratory thermometer (with an adult) instead.

topics.rl: During a fever, a digital thermometer under the tongue or in the armpit beeps when the reading is ready. School labs use laboratory thermometers to measure the temperature of water.

topics.h: Ice melts at 0 and water boils at 100. That's the clever idea behind the Celsius scale!
p: Temperature is commonly measured in degrees Celsius, written °C.
On the Celsius scale, pure water freezes (and ice melts) at 0 °C and water boils at 100 °C, at normal air pressure.
The scale is named after the Swedish scientist Anders Celsius.
The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K), but in daily life we mostly use °C. Some thermometers also show °F; normal body temperature is about 98.6 °F.
Weather reports give the day's maximum (highest) and minimum (lowest) temperatures in °C.

ex.q: In Shimla one winter morning it was 4 °C. By afternoon it was 13 °C. By how many degrees did the temperature rise?
st: Rise = afternoon temperature − morning temperature.

topics.rl: On the evening news you may hear: 'Today's maximum temperature was 41 °C and minimum 28 °C.' That is the Celsius scale at work.

topics.ch: A Journey through States of Water
topics.h: Water is a shape-shifter! It can be a hard ice cube, a splashing liquid or an invisible gas in the air.
p: Water can exist in three states: solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (water vapour).
A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume. An ice cube keeps its shape in any glass.
A liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape; it takes the shape of its container.
A gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume; it spreads out to fill all the space it gets. Water vapour is invisible.
All matter is made of tiny particles. In solids they are packed very close, in liquids a little apart, and in gases far apart and moving freely.

ex.q: Rohit pours 200 mL of water from a tall glass into a flat bowl. What changes and what stays the same?
st: Water is a liquid.
Liquids take the shape of their container, so the shape changes from tall to flat.
Liquids have a fixed volume, so the amount stays 200 mL.
ex.a: The shape changes, but the volume stays 200 mL.

topics.rl: In your kitchen you can see all three states of water: ice cubes from the freezer, water in a jug, and invisible water vapour rising from a boiling pot (the white mist you see is tiny droplets that formed as the vapour cooled).

rv.summary: Water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (water vapour). Solids have fixed shape and volume, liquids have fixed volume only, and gases have neither.

traps: Pouring a liquid changes its shape, not its volume.
Clouds and mist are not water vapour; they are tiny liquid droplets.

topics.ch: A Journey through States of Water
topics.h: Where does the water from wet clothes go? And where do the drops on a cold glass come from? Same water, opposite journeys!
p: Evaporation: liquid water slowly changes into water vapour from its surface. It happens at all temperatures, not only when water boils.
Evaporation is faster when it is hotter, when there is wind, when the water is spread over a larger area, and when the air is less humid (less moist).
Evaporation causes cooling: sweat cools our body, and water in an earthen matka or surahi stays cool as water seeping through it evaporates.
Condensation: water vapour cools and changes back into liquid water, like droplets on the outside of a cold glass, dew on grass, and a foggy bathroom mirror.
Water cycle: water evaporates from seas, rivers and land, condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds, and falls back as rain, snow or hail.

ex.q: Pooja hangs one wet dupatta spread out and another folded, both in the sun. Which dries first, and why?
st: Both are in the sun, so the temperature is the same.
The spread-out dupatta has a larger surface exposed to air.
A larger surface area makes evaporation faster.
ex.a: The spread-out dupatta dries first because more of its surface is open to the air.

topics.rl: On winter mornings in North India you can see dew drops on grass and leaves. In summer, a matka keeps drinking water cool without a fridge.

topics.ch: A Journey through States of Water
topics.h: Leave a kulfi out in May and see how fast it turns into a puddle! That's melting in action.
p: Melting: a solid changes into a liquid on heating. Ice melts at 0 °C.
Freezing: a liquid changes into a solid on cooling. Pure water freezes at 0 °C.
So melting and freezing are opposite changes, and for water both happen at 0 °C.
Boiling: water changes quickly into vapour at 100 °C, with bubbles forming throughout the liquid.
Water expands when it freezes, so ice is lighter than the same volume of water and floats. A glass bottle filled to the top with water can crack in a freezer.

ex.q: Ice cubes are put into a glass of water. Do they sink or float, and why?
st: When water freezes, it expands and takes up more space.
So a piece of ice is lighter than the same volume of water.
Things lighter than the same volume of water float.
ex.a: They float, because ice is lighter than the same volume of water.

topics.rl: Snow on the Himalayas melts in summer and feeds rivers like the Ganga. Kulfi and ice cream are made by freezing.

topics.ch: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
topics.h: Nani picks tiny stones out of the dal before cooking. She's doing science: separating a mixture!
p: A mixture has two or more substances mixed together. We separate them to remove unwanted or harmful parts, or to get useful parts.
Handpicking: picking out by hand things that are big enough to see and few in number, like stones from rice or dal.
Threshing: separating grains from their stalks by beating them, using animals, or using threshing machines.
Winnowing: dropping a mixture from a height in the wind. Light husk blows away; heavy grains fall close by. A soop (winnowing basket) is often used.
Sieving: passing a mixture through a sieve (chhalni). Fine particles pass through; bigger ones stay behind, like bran from flour or pebbles from sand.

ex.q: Grandpa has a sack of wheat grains mixed with light, dry husk. Which method should he use, and how does it work?
st: The husk is much lighter than the grains.
Winnowing uses wind to separate light and heavy parts.
He drops the mixture slowly from a height on a windy day: husk blows away, grains fall in a heap below.
ex.a: Winnowing

topics.rl: At a construction site, workers pass sand through a big slanting wire sieve to remove pebbles. At home, flour is sieved before making rotis.

topics.ch: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
topics.h: Muddy water from a village pond can be made clearer, step by step. Let's see how!
p: Sedimentation: when muddy water is left undisturbed, the heavier insoluble particles slowly settle at the bottom. The settled layer is called sediment.
Decantation: gently pouring off the clearer water from the top without disturbing the sediment.
Filtration: passing a mixture through a filter that lets the liquid pass but stops the solid particles. Examples: tea strainer, filter paper, a clean cotton cloth.
The clear liquid that passes through is called the filtrate; the solid left behind is the residue.
Filtered water may still have germs that we cannot see. It must be boiled or purified before drinking.

ex.q: While making paneer, Ammi adds lemon juice to hot milk (adult job!). Soft lumps form in a watery liquid. How can the paneer be separated?
st: The lumps (chhena) are solid; the watery part (whey) is liquid.
Pour the mixture through a clean muslin cloth.
The whey passes through; the paneer stays in the cloth.
ex.a: Filtration through a muslin cloth

topics.rl: Tea is filtered through a strainer every morning. Water purifiers at home and big water treatment plants use settling and filtering before cleaning the water further.

topics.ch: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
topics.t: Evaporation, churning and using methods together
topics.h: How do we get salt from the salty sea? The Sun helps us do it!
p: Evaporation can separate a solid dissolved in water: when the water evaporates, the solid is left behind.
Salt is made this way in salt pans along the coasts of states like Gujarat: seawater is let into shallow pans and the Sun evaporates the water, leaving salt.
Churning: curd or cream is churned (stirred hard) with a mathani or a churner. Butter, which is lighter, collects on top and is separated from buttermilk (chhaas).
Sometimes we use more than one method. Salt and sand: add water to dissolve the salt, filter out the sand, then evaporate the water to get the salt back.
Safety: heating to evaporate should only be done by or with an adult.

ex.q: Sana accidentally mixes salt with sand. How can she get both back?
st: Add water and stir: salt dissolves, sand does not.
Filter the mixture: sand stays on the filter paper as residue.
Leave the salty filtrate in a shallow dish in the sun (or let an adult heat it) so the water evaporates.
Salt is left behind in the dish.
ex.a: Dissolve in water, filter to get the sand, then evaporate the water to get the salt.

topics.rl: Making butter by churning curd is common in many Indian homes, and the leftover chhaas is a cool summer drink.

topics.h: A toy car moves, a cloud grows bigger, a candle 'breathes' air to burn. Are they alive? Let's find the real test!
p: Living things need food, water and air to live.
Living things breathe (take in air) and get energy from food. This is called respiration.
Living things grow, respond to changes around them (stimuli), get rid of wastes (excretion) and reproduce (make young ones of their own kind).
Most animals move from place to place; plants show movement too, like a chhui-mui (touch-me-not) folding its leaves when touched.
Living things have a life span: they are born, grow, grow old and die. Non-living things may show one or two of these features, but never all of them.

ex.q: A car moves and uses fuel. Is it a living thing?
st: A car moves and uses fuel, so it shows some features.
But it does not grow, breathe, reproduce or respond to touch on its own.
A living thing must show all the features of life.
ex.a: No. A car is non-living; it shows only a few features, not all.

topics.rl: When you water a wilting tulsi plant and it perks up, or a puppy runs to you when called, you are seeing living things respond.

topics.t: Seeds and plants are alive too
topics.h: A tiny dry moong seed looks lifeless. Add water, and in two days it sprouts! Was it alive all along?
p: A seed is a living thing that is resting. When conditions are right, it wakes up and starts to grow. This is called germination.
Seeds need water, air and a suitable (warm, not too cold) temperature to germinate.
Seeds kept dry do not germinate. Seeds kept fully under water (without air) usually do not germinate either. Seeds kept in a fridge germinate poorly or not at all.
Most seeds like moong and chana can germinate even in the dark.
Plants grow, take in air through tiny pores in their leaves, make their own food in sunlight, respond (roots grow towards water, shoots towards light) and make seeds.

ex.q: Arnav sets up three cups of moong seeds: A dry, B on wet cotton, C fully under water. Which sprout well and why?
st: Cup A has air and warmth but no water: no sprouting.
Cup B has water, air and warmth: good sprouting.
Cup C has water but very little air: little or no sprouting.
ex.a: Only cup B sprouts well, because seeds need water, air and suitable warmth.

topics.rl: Moong and chana sprouts are a healthy breakfast in many Indian homes. Soaking and keeping them in a damp cloth gives them water, air and warmth to germinate.

topics.h: A frog was once a tiny tadpole with a tail, and a butterfly was once a crawling caterpillar. Life is full of surprises!
p: A life cycle is the series of stages a living thing goes through from birth to becoming an adult that can produce young ones.
Frog: egg → tadpole (lives in water, has a tail, breathes with gills) → froglet (grows legs) → adult frog.
Mosquito: egg → larva → pupa → adult. The eggs, larvae and pupae live in still (stagnant) water, so we must not let water collect in coolers, pots or tyres.
Butterfly: egg → caterpillar (larva) → pupa (also called a chrysalis) → adult butterfly. Big changes in body shape like these are called metamorphosis.
Plant: seed → seedling → young plant → adult plant with flowers → fruits with seeds → new plants.

ex.q: Why do health workers ask people to empty water from coolers and old tyres every week, especially in the rainy season?
st: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water.
The larvae and pupae also grow in that water before becoming adults.
Emptying the water breaks the life cycle, so fewer mosquitoes are born.
ex.a: To stop mosquitoes from breeding, by removing the still water their eggs, larvae and pupae need.

topics.rl: During the monsoon you may see tadpoles in puddles and ponds. Silk is made from the cocoons that silkworms spin when they become pupae; they later turn into moths.

topics.h: The air you breathe, the water you drink and the sunshine on your face are gifts from nature. They are nature's treasures!
p: Natural resources are useful things we get from nature, like air, water, sunlight, soil, forests, minerals, coal and petroleum.
Things made by people from natural resources, like plastic, glass, paper and cement, are human-made materials.

Air is a mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen and about 21% oxygen, with small amounts of others like carbon dioxide and water vapour. We need oxygen to breathe; plants use carbon dioxide to make food.
Soil forms very, very slowly as rocks break down over many years; it holds plants and gives them water and minerals.
The Sun is the main source of energy on Earth: it gives light and warmth, and plants use sunlight to make food.

ex.q: Is a wooden chair a natural resource?
st: The wood comes from trees in forests, which are natural resources.
But the chair itself was cut, shaped and joined by people.
So the wood is natural, while the chair is a human-made object.
ex.a: No. The wood is a natural resource, but the chair is made by people from it.

topics.rl: Farmers depend on soil, water and sunlight; fishing families on the coast of Kerala depend on the sea; and the paper in your notebook came from trees.

topics.h: Some treasures refill themselves, like sunlight every day. Others took millions of years to form and will run out!
p: Renewable resources are replaced by nature in a short time, or will not run out: sunlight, wind, and water (renewed by the water cycle). Forests are renewable only if we plant new trees as we cut.
Non-renewable resources took a very long time to form and cannot be replaced quickly once used up: coal, petroleum, natural gas and minerals.
Coal, petroleum and natural gas are called fossil fuels. They formed from the remains of plants and animals buried deep under the Earth over millions of years.
Burning fossil fuels gives energy but also releases smoke and gases that pollute air.
Solar panels and windmills use renewable energy. India has big solar parks and wind farms.

ex.q: Why is coal called non-renewable when the Earth still has a lot of it?
st: Coal took millions of years to form from buried plants.
We are using it much, much faster than it can form again.
Once used up, it cannot be replaced in our lifetime.
ex.a: Because it takes millions of years to form, so it cannot be replaced once we use it up.

topics.rl: Rooftop solar panels on homes and schools turn sunlight into electricity, and windmills along the coasts of Tamil Nadu and Gujarat use wind.

rv.summary: Renewable resources like sunlight, wind and water are replaced by nature or will not run out. Non-renewable resources like coal, petroleum and natural gas took millions of years to form and cannot be replaced quickly.
focus: Sorting resources into renewable and non-renewable
How fossil fuels were formed
When forests count as renewable
Why solar and wind energy are better
remember: Renewable: sunlight, wind, water (water cycle)
Non-renewable: coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals
Fossil fuels formed from buried remains of plants and animals over millions of years
Petrol and diesel come from petroleum
traps: Forests are renewable only if new trees are planted.
Coal is non-renewable even though a lot is left; it cannot be replaced quickly.
Burning fossil fuels pollutes the air.

topics.h: If we keep taking from nature's treasure box without care, it will become empty. Let's be smart treasure keepers!
p: Conservation means using natural resources carefully so they last for future generations.
Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again) and Recycle (make new things from old) help save resources.
Save water: turn off taps, fix leaks, and collect rainwater (rainwater harvesting). Save electricity: switch off lights and fans when not needed.
Plant trees and protect forests. In the 1970s, villagers in the hills of present-day Uttarakhand hugged trees to stop them from being cut; this was the Chipko movement.
Walk, cycle or use public transport for short trips to save fuel and keep the air cleaner.

ex.q: Anu's family wants to save water at home. Which ideas work?
st: Turn off the tap while brushing teeth.
Fix leaking taps quickly.
Use a bucket instead of a running hose to wash the car, and reuse water from washing vegetables to water plants.
ex.a: All of these save water: closing taps, fixing leaks and reusing water.

topics.rl: Van Mahotsav, a tree-planting festival held every July in India, encourages people to plant trees. Many schools and homes now collect rainwater from rooftops.

rv.summary: Conservation means using natural resources carefully so they last. Reduce, reuse and recycle, saving water and electricity, planting trees and using less fuel all help.
focus: Meaning of conservation
Telling reduce, reuse and recycle apart
Ways to save water, electricity and fuel
The Chipko movement
remember: Reduce = use less; Reuse = use again; Recycle = make new things from old
Rainwater harvesting = collecting and storing rainwater
Chipko movement (1970s): villagers in present-day Uttarakhand hugged trees to save them
traps: Don't mix up reuse (same object again) and recycle (made into new things).
Using a cloth bag is reducing plastic, not recycling.

topics.h: On a clear night away from city lights, you can see thousands of stars. Some of them even make pictures in the sky!
p: Stars are huge balls of very hot gases that give out their own light and heat.
The Sun is a star. It looks big and bright because it is the star nearest to Earth; other stars look like tiny dots because they are very, very far away.

A constellation is a group of stars that seems to form a pattern or shape. Examples: Orion (also called Mriga), Ursa Major (whose seven bright stars are called Saptarishi or the Big Dipper) and Cassiopeia (shaped like a W or M).
The Pole Star (Dhruva tara) stays almost in the same place in the northern sky all night. Two stars of the Saptarishi, called pointer stars, point towards it.
Stars seem to move from east to west across the night sky because the Earth rotates from west to east. Bright city lights (light pollution) make stars hard to see.

ex.q: Kunal sees stars during the night but not during the day. Do the stars disappear in the daytime?
st: Stars are still in the sky during the day.
The Sun is so bright that its light makes the sky bright.
The faint light of distant stars cannot be seen against the bright sky.
ex.a: No. The stars are there, but the bright sunlight hides them.

topics.rl: Sailors and travellers once used the Pole Star to find the north direction at night. Today, stargazing camps in places like Ladakh, far from city lights, let people see the Milky Way.

rv.summary: Stars are huge balls of hot gases that give out their own light. The Sun is our nearest star. Constellations are star patterns, and the Pole Star helps us find north.
focus: What stars are and why they look tiny
Constellations: Orion, Ursa Major (Saptarishi), Cassiopeia
Finding north with the Pole Star and pointer stars
Apparent motion of stars and light pollution
remember: The Sun is a star, the one nearest to Earth
Saptarishi (Big Dipper) = seven bright stars of Ursa Major
Pole Star (Dhruva tara) stays almost fixed in the northern sky
Stars seem to move east to west because Earth rotates west to east
traps: Stars do not disappear in the day; bright sunlight hides them.
Stars are not small; they look tiny because they are very far away.
Stars do not really run across the sky; the Earth's rotation makes them seem to move.

topics.h: Our Earth is part of a giant family that circles around the Sun. Meet the family!
p: The Solar System has the Sun at its centre, with eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets going around it.
The eight planets in order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Planets do not make their own light; they shine by reflecting sunlight. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite and also shines with reflected sunlight.

Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. Venus is the hottest planet and the brightest planet in our night sky. Mars looks reddish. Jupiter is the largest planet. Saturn has beautiful rings.
Earth is the only planet known to have life. Since 2006, Pluto has been called a dwarf planet. Many asteroids orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.

ex.q: Lata says, 'The Moon is a star because it shines at night.' Is she right?
st: Stars make their own light.
The Moon does not make its own light; it reflects sunlight.
The Moon goes around the Earth, so it is Earth's natural satellite.
ex.a: No. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite, which shines by reflecting sunlight.

topics.rl: Venus is often seen as a very bright 'star' just after sunset or before sunrise. It is called the evening star or morning star, though it is actually a planet.

rv.summary: The Solar System has the Sun at its centre with eight planets, moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets. Planets and the Moon shine by reflecting sunlight.
focus: Order of the eight planets from the Sun
Special planets: smallest, largest, hottest, ringed, reddish
Planets and the Moon do not make their own light
Pluto as a dwarf planet and the asteroid belt
remember: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
Mercury: smallest, closest; Venus: hottest, brightest; Jupiter: largest
The Moon is Earth's natural satellite
Main asteroid belt: between Mars and Jupiter
traps: Don't say Mercury is the hottest; Venus is.
The Moon is not a star; it reflects sunlight.
Pluto is not counted as a planet since 2006; it is a dwarf planet.

topics.h: India sent a spacecraft to Mars on its very first try and landed near the Moon's south pole. Let's meet India's space heroes!
p: ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation) was set up in 1969. Dr Vikram Sarabhai is called the father of the Indian space programme.
Aryabhata, India's first satellite, was launched in 1975. Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian to travel to space in 1984.
Chandrayaan-1 (2008) helped discover water molecules on the Moon. Mangalyaan, the Mars Orbiter Mission, was launched in 2013 and reached Mars orbit in 2014; India succeeded on its first attempt.

Chandrayaan-3's lander Vikram touched down near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023, and the rover Pragyan explored the surface. India was the first country to land near the south pole. 23 August is now National Space Day in India.
Aditya-L1, launched in September 2023, is India's first mission to study the Sun. Many ISRO rockets are launched from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh.

ex.q: Put these Indian space events in order: Chandrayaan-3 landing, Aryabhata launch, Mangalyaan launch.
st: Aryabhata was launched in 1975.
Mangalyaan was launched in 2013.
Chandrayaan-3 landed in 2023.
ex.a: Aryabhata (1975) → Mangalyaan (2013) → Chandrayaan-3 landing (2023)

topics.rl: Satellites launched by ISRO help with weather forecasts, TV broadcasts, maps and warning people before cyclones.

rv.summary: ISRO was set up in 1969. India launched Aryabhata in 1975, reached Mars orbit on its first try with Mangalyaan, landed Chandrayaan-3 near the Moon's south pole in 2023 and launched Aditya-L1 to study the Sun.

What each mission studied or achieved

Aryabhata (1975); Rakesh Sharma in space (1984)
Mangalyaan launched 2013, reached Mars orbit 2014 on first attempt
Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023 (National Space Day)
