Chandrayaan-3 landed near the south pole, not the north pole.

qa.q: Which of these best describes science?
qa.a: A way of finding out how the world works
qa.e: Science is a method of exploring: observing, asking questions and testing ideas to understand the world.

qa.q: Tara wonders why ants walk in a line. What is she showing?
qa.e: Wondering 'why' about something you notice is curiosity, the starting point of science.

qa.q: What should a scientist do if a careful test shows their idea is wrong?
qa.e: Science grows by changing ideas when evidence shows they do not fit.

qa.q: Which of these is a question science can test?
qa.a: Do bean seeds sprout faster in warm water or cold water?
qa.e: We can test sprouting by setting up seeds and observing. The others depend on personal taste.

qa.q: Where can science be used?
qa.a: In the kitchen, the farm, the hospital and the playground
qa.e: Science is everywhere: in cooking, farming, medicine and even sports.

qa.q: Arjun says, 'Science is finished; everything is already known.' What is wrong with this?
qa.a: There are still many questions nobody has answered
qa.e: Scientists keep discovering new things every year. There is always more to find out.

qa.q: Which habit helps you most in science?
qa.e: Careful observation and questioning are the heart of scientific thinking.

qa.q: A farmer notices that plants near a tree grow less. She tries planting some in sunny spots to compare. What is she doing?
qa.a: Testing her idea, like a scientist
qa.e: She noticed something, made a guess (less sunlight) and set up a comparison to check it. That is scientific thinking.

qa.q: Which of these is an observation, not an opinion?
qa.a: The neem tree in our school is taller than the school wall
qa.e: An observation is something we can see or measure. Pretty, boring and love are personal feelings.

qa.q: Which tool helps you observe the tiny parts of a flower?
qa.e: A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger so we can see details.

qa.q: Why should a scientist record observations in a notebook?
qa.a: So the details are not forgotten and can be compared later
qa.e: Writing things down keeps the details safe so they can be checked and compared.

qa.q: Kabir finds an unknown white powder in the kitchen. What is the SAFE way to observe it?
qa.a: Look at it and ask an adult what it is
qa.e: Unknown substances can be harmful. Looking and asking an adult is safe; tasting or sniffing is not.

qa.q: Ananya notices that her tomato plant on the windowsill bends towards the window. Which is a good question to ask?
qa.a: Does the plant bend towards light?
qa.e: A good scientific question comes from the observation and can be tested, like placing the plant in different light.

qa.q: Which sense do you mainly use to observe that a koel is singing?
qa.e: A koel's song is a sound, so we observe it by hearing.

qa.q: Which is a more exact observation?
qa.e: Using a measurement with a unit gives an exact observation that others can check.

qa.q: Why do scientists ask questions after observing?
qa.a: Questions guide what to explore and test next
qa.e: A question gives a clear goal: what do we want to find out?

qa.q: What is a hypothesis?
qa.a: A smart guess that can be tested
qa.e: A hypothesis is a possible answer to a question, which we then test.

qa.q: Which step comes right after asking a question?
qa.e: After the question, we suggest a possible answer (hypothesis), then test it.

qa.q: Sana wants to test if sunlight helps methi seeds grow. What must she keep the same in both pots?
qa.a: Soil, water and type of seed
qa.e: In a fair test, only the thing being tested (sunlight) changes. Soil, water and seed must be the same.

qa.q: An experiment shows that a hypothesis was wrong. What should happen next?
qa.a: Make a new hypothesis and test again
qa.e: A wrong guess teaches us something. Scientists make a better guess and test again.

qa.q: Which is the LAST step of the scientific method?
qa.e: We draw a conclusion after studying the results of the experiment.

qa.q: Rohan tests whether salt or sugar dissolves faster. He uses hot water for salt and cold water for sugar. What is wrong?
qa.a: He changed two things, so the test is not fair
qa.e: He changed both the substance and the water temperature, so he cannot tell which one caused the difference.

qa.q: Why do scientists repeat an experiment?
qa.a: To check that the result is reliable
qa.e: Getting the same result again and again shows the result can be trusted.

qa.q: Which hypothesis can be tested?
qa.a: Ice melts faster in a sunny spot than in a shady spot
qa.e: We can time ice melting in sun and shade. Feelings like happy or sad cannot be measured.

qa.q: What does biodiversity mean?
qa.a: The variety of living things in a place
qa.e: 'Bio' means life. Biodiversity is the variety of all plants, animals and other living things.

qa.q: Which plant is a herb?
qa.e: Coriander is short with a soft green stem. Mango, peepal and banyan are tall trees.

qa.q: Which plant is a shrub?
qa.e: A rose bush has a woody stem with branches near the ground, so it is a shrub.

qa.q: A money plant growing up a wall with support is a:
qa.e: Plants that need support to climb upward are climbers.

qa.q: A watermelon plant spreads along the ground. It is a:
qa.e: Plants with weak stems that spread along the ground are creepers.

qa.q: What is special about a tree's stem?
qa.a: It is a thick, hard, woody trunk
qa.e: Trees have a strong woody trunk that holds them up tall, with branches higher up.

qa.q: Which of these regions in India is famous for its rich variety of plants and animals?
qa.e: The Western Ghats have forests full of many kinds of plants, frogs, birds and other animals.

qa.q: Why do we find different animals in different places?
qa.a: Each kind of animal is suited to where it lives
qa.e: Animals are suited to their surroundings: fish to water, camels to deserts, yaks to cold mountains.

qa.q: What kind of venation does a grass leaf have?
qa.e: In grass, the veins run side by side along the leaf. This is parallel venation.

qa.q: Which leaf has reticulate (net-like) venation?
qa.e: A hibiscus leaf has veins that branch out like a net.

qa.q: A taproot is:
qa.a: One main root with smaller side roots
qa.e: A taproot has a thick main root going down, with thin side roots.

qa.q: Which plant has fibrous roots?
qa.e: Maize has many thin roots of similar size from the base of the stem.

qa.q: Leaves with net-like veins usually go with which roots?
qa.e: Most plants with reticulate venation, like mango and mustard, have a taproot.

qa.q: Which seed splits into two parts when soaked?
qa.e: Soaked gram splits into two parts called cotyledons, so it is a dicot.

qa.q: Which animal has a backbone?
qa.e: A frog has a backbone. Earthworms, snails and butterflies do not.

qa.q: Why do scientists group living things?
qa.a: To make them easier to study and understand
qa.e: Grouping by shared features helps us learn about many living things quickly.

qa.q: What is an adaptation?
qa.a: A feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat
qa.e: Adaptations, like a fish's gills or a camel's long legs, help living things survive where they live.

qa.q: What does a camel's hump store?
qa.e: The hump stores fat, which the camel's body can use for energy when food is scarce.

qa.q: Why do cacti have spines instead of broad leaves?
qa.e: Broad leaves lose a lot of water. Spines lose very little, which helps in a dry desert.

qa.q: Which part helps a fish breathe in water?
qa.e: Gills take in oxygen that is dissolved in water.

qa.q: Why are deodar and pine trees cone-shaped with sloping branches?
qa.a: So that snow slides off easily
qa.e: Snow slides off the sloping branches instead of piling up and breaking them.

qa.q: Which animal is best suited to the cold mountains of Ladakh?
qa.e: A yak's long, thick hair keeps it warm in the cold mountains.

qa.q: How does the streamlined shape of a fish help it?
qa.a: It helps the fish move easily through water
qa.e: A streamlined body is smooth and pointed at the ends, so water flows past it easily.

qa.q: Which habitat is a lotus plant adapted to?
qa.e: Lotus leaves float on water, and the plant grows rooted in the mud of ponds and lakes.

qa.q: Which nutrient helps our body grow and repair itself?
qa.e: Proteins are called body-building foods because they help in growth and repair.

qa.q: Which food is rich in carbohydrates?
qa.e: Rice contains a lot of starch, which is a carbohydrate.

qa.q: Which food is a good source of protein?
qa.e: Pulses like moong dal are rich in protein.

qa.q: Which nutrient gives the MOST energy for the same amount of food?
qa.e: Fats give more than twice the energy of the same weight of carbohydrates or proteins.

qa.q: What does dietary fibre (roughage) do?
qa.a: Helps the body get rid of undigested food
qa.e: Fibre adds bulk and helps undigested food move out of the body, preventing constipation.

qa.q: Which test result shows that a food contains starch?
qa.a: It turns blue-black with dilute iodine solution
qa.e: Starch turns blue-black when a drop of dilute iodine solution is added.

qa.q: Rubbing a groundnut on paper leaves a patch that light shines through. What does this show?
qa.e: An oily patch that lets light through shows that fat is present.

qa.q: Why do we need water even though it gives no energy?
qa.a: It helps carry nutrients and remove wastes
qa.e: Water helps the body absorb nutrients and remove wastes through sweat and urine.

qa.q: What is a balanced diet?
qa.a: Food with all nutrients in the right amounts, plus fibre and water
qa.e: A balanced diet gives the body everything it needs in the right amounts.

qa.q: Which meal is the most balanced?
qa.a: Roti, dal, green sabzi, salad and curd
qa.e: This meal has carbohydrates (roti), protein (dal, curd), vitamins, minerals and fibre (sabzi, salad).

qa.q: Which of these is a millet?
qa.e: Ragi (finger millet) is a millet. Rice and wheat are other cereals, and potato is a tuber.

qa.q: Why should we eat junk food only rarely?
qa.a: It has too much fat, salt or sugar and few useful nutrients
qa.e: Junk food fills us up with fat, salt and sugar but lacks proteins, vitamins and fibre.

qa.q: Which is an example of mindful eating?
qa.a: Eating slowly and stopping when you feel full
qa.e: Paying attention while eating helps digestion and stops overeating.

qa.q: Who needs more energy-giving food?
qa.a: A farmer ploughing a field all day
qa.e: Hard physical work uses more energy, so a farmer working all day needs more energy food.

qa.q: The International Year of Millets was in which year?
qa.e: The United Nations named 2023 the International Year of Millets.

qa.q: Which habit helps reduce food waste?
qa.a: Taking only as much food as you can eat
qa.e: Taking small helpings and asking for more if needed means less food is thrown away.

qa.q: What causes a deficiency disease?
qa.a: Lack of a nutrient in the diet for a long time
qa.e: Deficiency diseases are caused by not getting enough of a nutrient over a long time, not by germs.

qa.q: Lack of vitamin C causes:
qa.e: Scurvy, with bleeding gums, is caused by a lack of vitamin C.

qa.q: A child with soft, bent bones may have rickets. Which vitamin is lacking?
qa.e: Vitamin D helps the body use calcium for strong bones. Its lack causes rickets.

qa.q: Which disease is caused by a lack of iodine?
qa.e: Lack of iodine causes goitre, a swelling of the neck. Iodised salt helps prevent it.

qa.q: Which food is a rich source of vitamin C?
qa.e: Amla (Indian gooseberry) is very rich in vitamin C.

qa.q: Night blindness is caused by a lack of:
qa.e: Vitamin A keeps our eyes healthy. Its lack causes night blindness.

qa.q: Meena feels tired and weak all the time, and her doctor says she has anaemia. What should she eat more of?
qa.a: Iron-rich foods like green leafy vegetables
qa.e: Anaemia is often caused by a lack of iron. Green leafy vegetables and pulses provide iron.

qa.q: How can deficiency diseases be prevented?
qa.e: A balanced diet supplies all the nutrients, so no deficiency develops.

qa.q: Which of these is attracted by a magnet?
qa.e: Iron is a magnetic material, so the nail is pulled by the magnet.

qa.q: Which metal is NOT attracted by a magnet?
qa.e: Copper is a metal, but it is non-magnetic.

qa.q: What is magnetite?
qa.a: A natural magnet found as a rock
qa.e: Magnetite, also called lodestone, is a naturally found rock that attracts iron.

qa.q: Materials that are NOT attracted by a magnet are called:
qa.e: Wood, plastic, glass and copper are examples of non-magnetic materials.

qa.q: Which group has ONLY magnetic materials?
qa.e: Iron, nickel and cobalt are all attracted by a magnet.

qa.q: Aditi drops iron pins into a box of sand. What is the easiest way to get them out?
qa.a: Move a magnet through the sand
qa.e: The magnet attracts the iron pins, leaving the sand behind.

qa.q: Which shape of magnet is shaped like the letter U?
qa.e: A U-shaped magnet is called a horseshoe magnet.

qa.q: Will a magnet pick up an aluminium soft-drink can?
qa.e: Aluminium is a metal but it is not attracted by a magnet.

qa.q: How many poles does every magnet have?
qa.e: Every magnet has two poles: north and south.

qa.q: What happens when the south pole of one magnet comes near the south pole of another?
qa.e: Like poles repel each other.

qa.q: Where is the attraction of a bar magnet the strongest?
qa.e: Iron filings gather mostly at the ends, showing the poles are strongest.

qa.q: A bar magnet is hung freely by a thread. In which direction will it come to rest?
qa.e: A freely suspended magnet always settles pointing north–south.

qa.q: Anu breaks a bar magnet into two pieces. What does each piece have?
qa.a: Both a north and a south pole
qa.e: Each piece becomes a complete magnet with two poles.

qa.q: Which pair of poles will attract each other?
qa.e: Unlike poles (N and S) attract each other.

qa.q: Which is the surest test that an object is a magnet?
qa.a: It repels one pole of a known magnet
qa.e: Iron is attracted by a magnet too, but only a magnet can repel another magnet. Repulsion is the sure test.

qa.q: Ravi has a magnet with its labels rubbed off. How can he find its north pole?
qa.a: Hang it freely; the end that points north is its north pole
qa.e: A freely hanging magnet points north–south. The end pointing north is the north pole.

qa.q: Why does a compass needle point north–south?
qa.a: The needle is a small magnet that can turn freely
qa.e: Like a freely hanging bar magnet, the magnetic needle comes to rest in the north–south direction.

qa.q: Who would find a compass most useful?
qa.a: A sailor in the middle of the sea
qa.e: Far out at sea there are no landmarks, so a compass shows the directions.

qa.q: How should you stroke an iron nail with a magnet to make it a magnet?
qa.a: With the same pole, in one direction, many times
qa.e: Stroking in only one direction, many times, lines up the nail's magnetism.

qa.q: Which of these can weaken a magnet?
qa.a: Heating it or dropping it often
qa.e: Heat, hammering and dropping make a magnet lose its magnetism.

qa.q: How should two bar magnets be stored?
qa.a: Side by side with unlike poles together, with keepers across the ends
qa.e: Unlike poles side by side with soft-iron keepers help magnets keep their strength.

qa.q: Sneha holds a compass near a strong magnet. What will happen to the needle?
qa.a: It will turn towards or away from the magnet
qa.e: The needle is a magnet, so it is attracted or repelled by the nearby magnet and stops showing the correct north.

qa.q: The marked end of a compass needle points towards a temple. In which direction is the temple?
qa.e: The marked end of the needle points north, so the temple is to the north.

qa.q: Why do compasses still matter even though we have phones with maps?
qa.a: A compass works without battery or signal
qa.e: In forests, mountains or at sea there may be no signal or charge, but a compass still works.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of length?
qa.e: The metre is the standard (SI) unit of length. Centimetre and kilometre are made from it.

qa.q: Why are handspans not good for measuring accurately?
qa.a: Different people have different handspan lengths
qa.e: Each person's handspan is a different length, so results do not match.

qa.q: How many centimetres are there in 4 m?
How many millimetres are in 7 cm?
qa.e: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 7 cm = 7 × 10 = 70 mm.

qa.q: Ravi's school is 3 km from home. How far is that in metres?
Which unit is best to measure the length of a pencil?
qa.e: A pencil is about 15 to 20 cm long, so centimetres suit it best.

qa.q: Which old unit is the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger?
qa.e: A cubit is measured from the elbow to the fingertip.

qa.q: A rope is 1 m 50 cm long. How many centimetres is that?
Where should your eye be when you read a scale?
qa.e: Looking from the side makes the mark seem shifted, giving a wrong reading.

qa.q: A leaf starts at 1.0 cm and ends at 7.5 cm on a ruler. What is its length?
Which tool is best to measure around the trunk of a mango tree?
qa.e: A flexible measuring tape can wrap around a curved trunk.

qa.q: How can you measure the length of a curved line on a map?
qa.a: Lay a thread along it and then measure the thread
qa.e: The thread follows every curve. When straightened, its length can be read on a ruler.

qa.q: Kriti's ruler has a broken zero, so she starts measuring her eraser at the 3 cm mark. The eraser ends at 8 cm. How long is it?
qa.e: Length = 8 − 3 = 5 cm.

qa.q: Why should the scale touch the object along its length?
qa.e: If the scale is lifted or tilted, the marks do not line up with the ends of the object.

qa.q: Ayaan measures a book and gets 24.5 cm. What does the '.5' mean?
qa.e: Each centimetre has 10 mm, so 0.5 cm = 5 mm. The book is 24 cm and 5 mm long.

qa.q: Which is a correct way to measure the length of a classroom?
qa.a: Use a long measuring tape laid straight along the floor
qa.e: A long tape laid straight gives an accurate measurement of a big length.

qa.q: A stone dropped from a building shows which type of motion?
qa.e: The stone falls straight down, along a straight line.

qa.q: Which is an example of circular motion?
qa.a: A giant wheel turning at a mela
qa.e: The seats of a giant wheel move in a circle around its centre.

qa.q: What is periodic motion?
qa.a: Motion that repeats after fixed intervals of time
qa.e: Periodic motion repeats itself regularly, like a pendulum or a clock's hands.

qa.q: A swinging pendulum shows:
qa.e: A pendulum moves to and fro, repeating after equal intervals of time.

qa.q: The tip of a ceiling fan blade moves in a circle and repeats. Its motion is:
qa.e: It moves around a circle and returns to the same point again and again, so it is circular and periodic.

qa.q: A girl sitting in a moving bus is at rest compared to which of these?
qa.e: Her position does not change compared to her seat, but it changes compared to things outside.

qa.q: A sprinter running in a 100 m race on a straight track shows:
qa.e: On a straight track, the runner moves along a straight line.

qa.q: Which of these shows periodic motion?
qa.e: A vibrating string moves to and fro again and again, so its motion is periodic.

qa.q: What is the material of an object?
qa.a: What the object is made of
qa.e: A material is the substance an object is made of, like wood, glass or metal.

qa.q: Which material is lustrous?
qa.e: Gold has a natural shine, so it is lustrous.

qa.q: Which of these is a soft material?
qa.e: A sponge can be pressed easily, so it is soft.

qa.q: Why does an old copper vessel look dull?
qa.a: Its surface has changed due to air and moisture
qa.e: Metals lose their shine when their surface reacts with air and moisture. Cleaning brings back the shine.

qa.q: Which object can be made from wood, plastic or metal?
qa.e: Chairs can be made of many materials, showing one object can be made of different materials.

qa.q: Which group shows objects all made from wood?
qa.e: Pencils, doors and cricket bats are usually made from wood.

qa.q: Which is a hard material?
qa.e: Iron is difficult to press or scratch, so it is hard.

qa.q: Aluminium foil is shiny. This property is called:
qa.e: The shine of a material is called lustre.

qa.q: Which material is soluble in water?
qa.e: Sugar dissolves completely in water and disappears from view.

qa.q: What happens when you pour a little cooking oil into water?
qa.a: It forms a layer on top of the water
qa.e: Oil does not mix with water and floats as a separate layer.

qa.q: Which object will sink in water?
qa.e: An iron nail sinks, while a dry leaf, cork and thermocol float.

qa.q: Butter paper lets you see objects only partly. It is:
qa.e: Translucent materials let some light through, so things look blurry.

qa.q: Which material is opaque?
qa.e: We cannot see through cardboard at all, so it is opaque.

qa.q: Why are window panes usually made of clear glass?
qa.a: Glass is transparent and lets light in
qa.e: Transparent glass lets light in and lets us see outside.

qa.q: A bathroom window uses frosted glass. Why?
qa.a: It lets light in but people cannot see clearly inside
qa.e: Frosted glass is translucent: light comes in, but you cannot see clearly through it.

qa.q: Kiran stirs chalk powder in water and leaves it. What will she find after some time?
qa.a: The chalk powder settles at the bottom
qa.e: Chalk is insoluble, so it does not dissolve and slowly settles down.

qa.q: Why do we group materials?
qa.a: To study them easily and find what we need
qa.e: Grouping by properties makes it easier to compare materials and choose the right one.

qa.q: Which property makes glass good for windows?
qa.e: Transparent glass lets light and sight pass through.

qa.q: Which group of materials is all transparent?
qa.e: We can see clearly through clear glass, clean water and air.

qa.q: Which material is best for making a raincoat?
qa.a: Plastic, because water does not pass through it
qa.e: Plastic does not let water through, which keeps you dry.

qa.q: Glass is transparent, hard and does not dissolve in water. What does this show?
qa.a: One material can belong to many groups
qa.e: Every material has many properties, so it fits into many groups at once.

qa.q: Which of these objects is made of a material that is both lustrous and hard?
qa.e: A clean iron nail is shiny (lustrous) and hard.

qa.q: Why are diyas and matkas made from wet clay?
qa.a: Wet clay is soft and easy to shape, and it becomes hard after baking
qa.e: Soft wet clay can be moulded into shapes. Once baked, it is hard and holds its shape.

qa.q: Which material would you choose for a boat's float?
qa.a: A material that floats, like wood or thermocol
qa.e: A float must stay on top of the water, so it needs a material that floats.

qa.q: What does temperature tell us?
qa.a: How hot or cold something is
qa.e: Temperature is a measure of the degree of hotness or coldness.

qa.q: Why can't we rely on touch to judge temperature?
qa.a: The same thing can feel hot or cold depending on what we touched before
qa.e: Our skin compares with its previous feeling, so touch can mislead us.

qa.q: Which instrument measures temperature?
qa.e: A thermometer measures how hot or cold something is.

qa.q: Rani keeps one hand in cold water and one in warm water, then dips both in tap water. What does the hand from cold water feel?
qa.e: Compared with the cold water it was in, the tap water feels warm to that hand.

qa.q: Which is the safest way to find out if bath water is too hot?
qa.a: Ask an adult to check with a thermometer
qa.e: A thermometer gives a safe, correct reading without risking a burn.

qa.q: Which of these is the coldest?
qa.e: Ice from a freezer has the lowest temperature among these.

qa.q: Which word describes water that is slightly warm?
qa.e: Lukewarm means slightly warm, not hot.

qa.q: A doctor wants to know if Arjun has a fever. What will the doctor use?
qa.e: Touch can mislead us, so a doctor uses a thermometer to get the exact temperature.

qa.q: What is the normal temperature of the human body, in °C?
qa.e: The normal body temperature is about 37 °C.

qa.q: What is the usual range of a clinical thermometer?
qa.e: Body temperature stays within a small range, so a clinical thermometer reads from 35 °C to 42 °C.

qa.q: Which thermometer would you use to measure the temperature of hot water in a lab?
qa.e: A laboratory thermometer has a range of about −10 °C to 110 °C, suitable for hot water.

qa.q: Why are digital thermometers preferred over mercury thermometers?
qa.a: Mercury is poisonous if the thermometer breaks
qa.e: Mercury is toxic and harmful if a glass thermometer breaks. Digital ones avoid this.

qa.q: When reading a laboratory thermometer in water, you should:
qa.a: Read it while the bulb is still in the water
qa.e: Once taken out, the reading starts to change. Read it while the bulb is in the water.

qa.q: Kabir's thermometer shows 39 °C. What does this suggest?
qa.e: 39 °C is higher than the normal 37 °C, so he likely has a fever.

qa.q: Why should you wash a clinical thermometer before and after use?
qa.e: Washing removes germs so that infections do not spread.

qa.q: What is the usual range of a laboratory thermometer?
qa.e: A laboratory thermometer reads from about −10 °C to 110 °C.

qa.q: At what temperature does pure water boil at normal air pressure, in °C?
qa.e: Water boils at 100 °C at normal air pressure.

qa.q: At what temperature does ice melt, in °C?
qa.e: Ice melts, and pure water freezes, at 0 °C.

qa.q: The Celsius scale is named after:
qa.e: Anders Celsius was a Swedish scientist who proposed the scale.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of temperature?
qa.e: The kelvin (K) is the SI unit, though °C is used more in daily life.

qa.q: A weather report says the maximum temperature was 38 °C and the minimum 26 °C. What is the difference, in °C?
qa.e: Difference = 38 − 26 = 12 °C.

qa.q: The temperature in a town was 15 °C at 6 am and 24 °C at 2 pm. By how much did it rise, in °C?
Normal body temperature is about 37 °C. About what is it in °F?
qa.e: 37 °C is the same as about 98.6 °F on the Fahrenheit scale.

qa.q: How many degrees are there between the freezing point and boiling point of water on the Celsius scale?
qa.e: From 0 °C to 100 °C is 100 degrees.

qa.q: What are the three states of water?
qa.e: Water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (water vapour).

qa.q: Which state has a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
qa.e: A solid, like an ice cube, keeps its shape and volume.

qa.q: Which state takes the shape of its container but has a fixed volume?
qa.e: Liquids flow and take the container's shape, but their volume does not change.

qa.q: Why can't we see water vapour in the air?
qa.a: It is a gas and is invisible
qa.e: Water vapour is an invisible gas. Clouds and mist are tiny liquid droplets.

qa.q: In which state are the particles farthest apart?
qa.e: Gas particles are far apart and move freely, which is why gases spread out.

qa.q: A gas spreads out to fill:
qa.a: All the space available to it
qa.e: Gases have no fixed volume, so they fill any space they get.

qa.q: Which of these is water in the solid state?
qa.e: A hailstone is a ball of ice, which is solid water.

qa.q: Meera pours 1 litre of milk from a jug into a round pot. What is the volume in the pot?
qa.e: A liquid keeps its volume when poured, so it is still 1 litre.

qa.q: What is evaporation?
qa.a: Liquid water changing into water vapour
qa.e: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface.

qa.q: Why do drops of water appear on the outside of a glass of iced water?
qa.a: Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold glass
qa.e: The cold glass cools the water vapour in the surrounding air, and it changes into droplets.

qa.q: On which day will wet clothes dry the fastest?
qa.a: A hot, sunny and windy day
qa.e: Heat, wind and dry air all make evaporation faster.

qa.q: Why does water in an earthen matka stay cool?
qa.a: Water seeping out through tiny pores evaporates and cools the pot
qa.e: Evaporation takes heat from the pot and the water, cooling them.

qa.q: Dew drops on grass on a winter morning are formed by:
qa.e: Water vapour in the air cools at night and condenses on the cool grass.

qa.q: Does evaporation happen only when water boils?
qa.a: No, it happens at all temperatures
qa.e: A puddle dries on a normal day without boiling. Evaporation goes on at all temperatures.

qa.q: How are clouds formed?
qa.a: Water vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets
qa.e: Rising water vapour cools high up and condenses into tiny droplets that make clouds.

qa.q: Why do we feel cool when sweat dries on our skin?
qa.a: Evaporation of sweat takes away heat from the body
qa.e: As sweat evaporates, it takes heat from our body, so we feel cooler.

qa.q: What is melting?
qa.a: A solid changing into a liquid
qa.e: When ice is heated, it melts into water: solid to liquid.

qa.q: At what temperature does pure water freeze, in °C?
qa.e: Pure water freezes at 0 °C, the same temperature at which ice melts.

qa.q: Water kept in the freezer turns into ice. This is:
qa.e: A liquid changing into a solid on cooling is freezing.

qa.q: Why does ice float on water?
qa.a: Ice is lighter than the same volume of water
qa.e: Water expands on freezing, so ice is lighter than the same volume of water and floats.

qa.q: Why can a glass bottle filled to the top with water crack in the freezer?
qa.e: As water turns to ice it takes up more space and pushes on the bottle.

qa.q: Melting and freezing are:
qa.e: Melting is solid to liquid; freezing is liquid to solid. They are opposites.

qa.q: A kulfi left on a plate on a hot day turns into a liquid. What has happened?
qa.e: Heat from the surroundings turns the solid kulfi into liquid: melting.

qa.q: How does boiling differ from evaporation?
qa.a: Boiling happens quickly at a fixed temperature with bubbles throughout; evaporation happens slowly from the surface at any temperature
qa.e: Water boils at 100 °C with bubbles inside the liquid, while evaporation goes on quietly from the surface at any temperature.

qa.q: Which method is best to remove a few small stones from rice?
qa.e: The stones are few and easy to see, so they can be picked out by hand.

qa.q: What is threshing?
qa.e: Threshing beats the harvested stalks so the grains come off.

qa.q: In winnowing, why does the husk fly away?
qa.a: It is lighter than the grains
qa.e: The wind carries the light husk away, while heavy grains fall down near the person.

qa.q: Which tool is used for sieving flour at home?
qa.e: A chhalni has tiny holes that let fine flour pass and stop the bran.

qa.q: Why do we need to separate substances from a mixture?
qa.a: To remove unwanted or harmful parts and to get useful ones
qa.e: We remove stones from dal and husk from grain so food is clean and useful.

qa.q: At a construction site, workers separate pebbles from sand by:
qa.e: Sand passes through the holes of a big sieve, and pebbles stay behind.

qa.q: Which method needs wind to work?
qa.e: Winnowing uses moving air to carry away the light husk.

qa.q: Handpicking is useful only when:
qa.a: The unwanted pieces are big enough to see and are few
qa.e: We can pick by hand only things we can see and that are not too many.

qa.q: What is sedimentation?
qa.a: Heavier insoluble particles settling down in a liquid
qa.e: When a mixture is left still, heavy particles like mud settle at the bottom.

qa.q: Pouring off clear water without disturbing the settled mud is called:
qa.e: Decantation means gently pouring the liquid away from the sediment.

qa.q: Which method separates tea leaves from tea?
qa.e: A tea strainer is a filter: the liquid tea passes and the leaves stay.

qa.q: After filtering, the solid left on the filter paper is called the:
qa.e: The solid that stays on the filter is the residue; the liquid that passes is the filtrate.

qa.q: Is filtered water always safe to drink?
qa.a: No, it may still have germs, so it should be boiled or purified
qa.e: Germs are too tiny to be stopped by simple filters, so water must be boiled or purified.

qa.q: Which of these can be separated by sedimentation and decantation?
qa.e: Sand is insoluble and heavy, so it settles and the water can be poured off.

qa.q: How is paneer separated from whey at home?
qa.a: By filtering through a muslin cloth
qa.e: The muslin cloth lets the whey pass and holds back the paneer.

qa.q: Why is filtration usually done after sedimentation and decantation?
qa.a: Most of the mud is removed first, so the filter does not get blocked quickly
qa.e: Removing most of the mud first means the filter only has to catch the smaller particles left behind.

qa.q: How is salt obtained from seawater?
qa.e: The Sun evaporates the water from seawater in shallow pans, leaving salt behind.

qa.q: Can filtration separate salt that is dissolved in water?
qa.a: No, dissolved salt passes through the filter
qa.e: Dissolved particles are mixed in the water and go through the filter. Evaporation is needed.

qa.q: Which method is used to get butter from curd?
qa.e: Churning makes the butter separate and collect on top.

qa.q: What is the correct order to separate a mixture of salt and sand?
qa.e: Dissolving frees the salt into water, filtering removes the sand, and evaporating gives back the salt.

qa.q: Why does butter collect on top when curd is churned?
qa.e: Butter is lighter than buttermilk, so it floats up and gathers on top.

qa.q: Sugar is dissolved in water. How can you get the sugar back?
qa.e: When the water evaporates, the sugar is left behind.

qa.q: Where in India is salt commonly made from seawater?
qa.a: In salt pans along the coast of Gujarat
qa.e: Coastal areas like Gujarat have salt pans where seawater evaporates in the sun.

qa.q: What is left in the dish when salty water evaporates?
qa.e: The water turns to vapour and the dissolved salt stays behind.

qa.q: Which feature is shown by ALL living things?
qa.e: Every living thing needs food for energy: plants make their own, animals eat it. Legs, wings and leaves are found only in some.

qa.q: A chhui-mui (touch-me-not) folds its leaves when touched. This shows that plants:
qa.e: Folding leaves after a touch is a response to a stimulus.

qa.q: Why is a cloud NOT a living thing, even though it grows bigger?
qa.a: It does not breathe, eat or reproduce
qa.e: Growing alone is not enough. A cloud does not show the other features of life.

qa.q: What is respiration?
qa.a: Breathing and getting energy from food
qa.e: In respiration, living things use air to release energy from food.

qa.q: Getting rid of wastes from the body is called:
qa.e: Excretion removes harmful waste materials from the body.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-living thing?
qa.e: A bicycle can be moved, but it does not breathe, grow or reproduce.

qa.q: Living things have a life span. This means they:
qa.a: Are born, grow, grow old and die
qa.e: Every living thing goes through stages and finally dies.

qa.q: Do plants need air?
qa.e: All living things, including plants, need air for respiration.

qa.q: What is germination?
qa.a: A seed starting to sprout and grow
qa.e: Germination is when a resting seed wakes up and begins to grow.

qa.q: Which conditions do seeds need to germinate?
qa.a: Water, air and a suitable temperature
qa.e: Seeds need water, air and suitable warmth. Many sprout even without soil or light.

qa.q: Why do seeds kept fully under water usually not germinate?
qa.e: Seeds need air too. Under water, they get very little air.

qa.q: Seeds were kept on wet cotton in a fridge. They did not sprout. Why?
qa.e: They had water and air, but the cold temperature stopped germination.

qa.q: Is a dry seed living or non-living?
qa.e: A dry seed is alive but resting. With the right conditions it germinates.

qa.q: Which shows that plants respond to their surroundings?
qa.e: Bending towards light is a response to a stimulus.

qa.q: Plants take in air through:
qa.e: Leaves have tiny pores through which air goes in and out.

qa.q: Riya wants moong sprouts for breakfast. What should she do?
qa.a: Soak the seeds and keep them in a damp cloth
qa.e: Soaking gives water, and a damp cloth keeps air and warmth, so they germinate.

qa.q: Which is the correct life cycle of a frog?
qa.e: A frog hatches from an egg as a tadpole, grows legs as a froglet, then becomes an adult.

qa.q: Where do mosquitoes lay their eggs?
qa.e: Mosquito eggs, larvae and pupae all develop in still water.

qa.q: What is the larva of a butterfly called?
qa.e: The butterfly larva is a caterpillar that eats leaves and grows.

qa.q: How does a tadpole breathe?
qa.e: Tadpoles live in water and breathe using gills.

qa.q: Which stage comes just before the adult in a mosquito's life cycle?
qa.e: The order is egg → larva → pupa → adult.

qa.q: What is metamorphosis?
qa.a: A big change in body shape during the life cycle
qa.e: A caterpillar turning into a butterfly or a tadpole into a frog is metamorphosis.

qa.q: Which is the correct life cycle of a plant?
qa.a: Seed → seedling → adult plant → flowers → fruits with seeds
qa.e: A seed germinates into a seedling, grows into an adult plant, flowers, and makes fruits with seeds.

qa.q: How does emptying water from a cooler every week help?
qa.e: Removing still water breaks the mosquito life cycle before larvae become adults.

qa.q: Which of these is a natural resource?
qa.e: Water comes directly from nature. Plastic, glass and cement are made by people.

qa.q: Which gas makes up the largest part of air?
qa.e: Nitrogen is about 78% of air; oxygen is about 21%.

qa.q: About what percentage of air is oxygen?
qa.e: Oxygen makes up about 21% of air.

qa.q: What is the main source of energy for life on Earth?
qa.e: The Sun gives light and heat, and plants use sunlight to make food for all living things.

qa.q: How is soil formed?
qa.a: Very slowly, as rocks break down over many years
qa.e: Soil forms very slowly as rocks break into tiny bits mixed with remains of plants and animals.

qa.q: Which gas do plants take in to make their food?
qa.e: Plants use carbon dioxide from air, water and sunlight to make food.

qa.q: Paper is made from trees. Paper is:
qa.a: A human-made material from a natural resource
qa.e: Trees are natural; people make paper from wood pulp.

qa.q: Which of these do forests give us?
qa.a: Wood, fruits, medicines and a home for wildlife
qa.e: Forests give many useful things and are home to many animals.

qa.q: Which is a renewable resource?
qa.e: The Sun keeps shining, so sunlight will not run out.

qa.q: Which is a non-renewable resource?
qa.e: Coal took millions of years to form and cannot be replaced quickly.

qa.q: How were fossil fuels formed?
qa.a: From remains of plants and animals buried over millions of years
qa.e: Buried remains changed slowly under heat and pressure into coal, petroleum and natural gas.

qa.q: Which of these is a fossil fuel?
qa.e: Natural gas, like coal and petroleum, is a fossil fuel.

qa.q: When can forests be called renewable?
qa.a: Only if new trees are planted as old ones are cut
qa.e: Forests grow back only if we replant and cut wisely.

qa.q: Why should we use more solar and wind energy?
qa.a: They are renewable and cause less pollution
qa.e: Sun and wind will not run out and do not release smoke like burning coal.

qa.q: Petrol and diesel are obtained from:
qa.e: Petrol and diesel are made by refining petroleum.

qa.q: Water is called renewable because:
qa.a: The water cycle keeps renewing it
qa.e: Water evaporates, forms clouds and falls as rain again. But clean fresh water is limited, so we must still save it.

qa.q: What does conservation of natural resources mean?
qa.a: Using them carefully so they last for the future
qa.e: Conservation is careful, wise use so resources last.

qa.q: Using an old jam jar as a pencil holder is an example of:
qa.e: Using the same object again for another purpose is reusing.

qa.q: Turning old newspapers into new paper is:
qa.e: Recycling turns used materials into new products.

qa.q: What was the Chipko movement?
qa.a: Villagers hugging trees to stop them from being cut
qa.e: In the 1970s, villagers in the hills of present-day Uttarakhand hugged trees to protect forests.

qa.q: Which is a good way to save water?
qa.a: Turning off the tap while brushing
qa.e: Closing the tap while brushing saves many litres of water.

qa.q: What is rainwater harvesting?
qa.a: Collecting and storing rainwater for later use
qa.e: Rooftop rainwater is collected in tanks or sent underground to recharge wells.

qa.q: Which habit helps save fuel?
qa.a: Cycling or walking for short distances
qa.e: Cycling and walking use no fuel and keep the air cleaner.

qa.q: Carrying a cloth bag to the market instead of taking new plastic bags helps to:
qa.e: Using less plastic means less waste. That is 'reduce'.

qa.q: What is a star?
qa.a: A huge ball of hot gases that gives out its own light
qa.e: Stars, like the Sun, are huge balls of hot gases that make light and heat.

qa.q: Which star is nearest to the Earth?
qa.e: The Sun is a star, and it is the closest star to us.

qa.q: Why do stars look like tiny dots?
qa.e: Many stars are huge, some bigger than the Sun, but they are extremely far away.

qa.q: What is a constellation?
qa.a: A group of stars that seems to form a pattern
qa.e: Constellations are star patterns like Orion and Ursa Major.

qa.q: The Saptarishi is part of which constellation?
qa.e: The seven bright stars of Ursa Major are called Saptarishi or the Big Dipper.

qa.q: Which star helps us find the north direction at night?
qa.e: The Pole Star stays almost fixed in the northern sky.

qa.q: Why do stars seem to move from east to west at night?
qa.a: Because the Earth rotates from west to east
qa.e: As the Earth spins, the stars appear to move the opposite way across the sky.

qa.q: Why can we see more stars in a village than in a big city?
qa.a: There are fewer bright lights in a village
qa.e: City lights brighten the sky (light pollution), hiding faint stars.

qa.q: How many planets are there in our Solar System?
qa.e: There are eight planets. Pluto was renamed a dwarf planet in 2006.

qa.q: Which is the largest planet?
qa.e: Jupiter is the biggest planet in the Solar System.

qa.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
qa.e: Mercury is the first planet from the Sun.

qa.q: Which planet is the hottest?
qa.e: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick atmosphere traps heat.

qa.q: What is the Moon?
qa.e: The Moon goes around the Earth and reflects sunlight; it is a natural satellite.

qa.q: Why do planets shine in the night sky?
qa.e: Planets do not make light; they reflect light from the Sun.

qa.q: Which planet comes right after Earth, moving away from the Sun?
qa.e: The order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars...

qa.q: Where is the main belt of asteroids found?
qa.e: Most asteroids go around the Sun in a belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

qa.q: In which year was India's first satellite, Aryabhata, launched?
qa.e: Aryabhata was launched in 1975.

qa.q: Who was the first Indian to travel to space?
qa.e: Rakesh Sharma went to space in 1984.

qa.q: Which Indian mission studies the Sun?
qa.e: 'Aditya' is a name for the Sun. Aditya-L1 was launched in 2023 to study it.

qa.q: Where did Chandrayaan-3's lander touch down?
qa.e: Vikram landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023.

qa.q: Which day is celebrated as National Space Day in India?
qa.e: It marks the day Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon in 2023.

qa.q: What was special about Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission)?
qa.a: India reached Mars orbit on its first attempt
qa.e: India's Mars Orbiter Mission reached Mars orbit in 2014 on the very first try.

qa.q: Who is known as the father of the Indian space programme?
qa.e: Dr Vikram Sarabhai led the setting up of India's space programme.

qa.q: In which year was ISRO set up?
qa.e: ISRO was set up in 1969.
